name: Inferior vena cava
func: The body's largest vein. It returns oxygen-poor blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen up to the right atrium of the heart, running to the right of the aorta along the back of the abdomen.

levels.kid:
The **inferior vena cava** is the biggest vein in your body. "Inferior" means "lower," because it brings back blood from the bottom half of you: your legs, feet, tummy and belly organs.

It's a big, wide tube that runs up the back of your tummy, right beside your backbone, next to the aorta, which is the big artery going down. So they're like two highways side by side, one going down and one coming up!

The inferior vena cava passes through the big breathing muscle under your lungs and pours its blood into the bottom of the heart's upper-right room.
levels.hs:
The **inferior vena cava (IVC)** forms at about the level of the **L5** vertebra, where the **left and right common iliac veins** join, slightly below and to the right of where the aorta splits.

It runs up the back wall of the abdomen on the **right side** of the vertebral column, to the **right of the abdominal aorta**. Higher up, it sits in a groove on the back of the **liver**. It passes through the **diaphragm** at about **T8**, through an opening in the diaphragm's central tendon (the **caval opening**), and almost immediately enters the bottom of the **right atrium**.

Tributaries include the **lumbar veins**, the **renal veins** from the kidneys, the right adrenal vein and, just under the diaphragm, the **hepatic veins** from the liver. Notably, blood from the stomach and intestines does **not** go straight into the IVC: it detours through the liver via the hepatic portal vein first.

The IVC is up to about 2.5 cm wide and is the largest vein in the body. Like the SVC, it has no working valves in adults.
levels.college:
Asymmetry explains several tributaries: the **left renal vein** is long and crosses in front of the aorta (just below the SMA) to reach the IVC, and it also receives the **left adrenal vein**; on the right, the shorter renal vein and the right adrenal vein drain directly into the IVC. This is why left-sided veins are longer and why surgeons prefer the left kidney for living donation.

Because the caval opening is in the **central tendon**, contraction of the diaphragm during inspiration **widens** it, helping venous return; by contrast the esophageal opening is narrowed by muscle and the aortic hiatus is unaffected.

At the right atrium, a fold called the **Eustachian valve** (valve of the IVC) directs inflowing blood; before birth it steered oxygen-rich blood arriving from the umbilical vein across the foramen ovale to the left heart.

Collateral routes if the IVC is blocked include the **ascending lumbar–azygos/hemiazygos** pathway, the vertebral venous plexuses and superficial abdominal wall veins. Unlike portal hypertension collaterals, caval collaterals on the abdominal wall flow **upward** below the umbilicus.

On bedside ultrasound, the IVC's diameter and how much it collapses when breathing in (or sniffing) help estimate **right atrial pressure** and fluid status.
levels.phd:
The IVC has one of the most complicated embryological histories of any vessel. It forms in sequence from three paired venous systems: the **posterior cardinal**, **subcardinal** and **supracardinal veins**, plus the **hepatic (vitelline)** segment. Simplified: the hepatic segment comes from the right vitelline vein; the suprarenal segment from the right subcardinal; the renal segment from subcardinal–supracardinal anastomoses; and the infrarenal segment from the right supracardinal vein.

Because so many pieces must regress or persist correctly, variants are common. A **left-sided IVC** (persistent left supracardinal) occurs in about 0.2–0.5% of people; a **duplicated IVC** in about 0.2–3%. A **circumaortic** or **retroaortic left renal vein** reflects persistence of other anastomoses. **Azygos continuation of the IVC**, where the hepatic segment fails to form and blood returns via a huge azygos vein, is associated with heterotaxy syndromes. These variants matter for surgeons and for placing IVC filters.

Hemodynamically, venous return from the lower body is aided by the **calf muscle pump** (deep veins with valves compressed by muscle) and the **respiratory pump**: during inspiration, abdominal pressure rises as thoracic pressure falls, squeezing blood from the abdominal IVC into the chest. Venous thrombosis follows **Virchow's triad**: stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Most leg clots begin behind venous valve cusps, where flow is slow and oxygen tension low, promoting endothelial activation and tissue factor expression.
levels.expert:
**Deep vein thrombosis** can extend into the IVC, causing bilateral leg swelling; a clot that breaks off travels through the IVC to cause **pulmonary embolism**. When anticoagulation is unsafe, such as soon after brain surgery or an intracranial bleed, an **IVC filter** can be placed by catheter, usually below the renal veins, to trap large emboli; filters carry their own risks (filter thrombosis, migration) and are removed when no longer needed.

**IVC compression** by large abdominal tumors or masses lowers venous return and blood pressure, and the **prone position** in spinal surgery can compress the abdomen and raise IVC pressure. That pressure is transmitted through the valveless **vertebral venous (Batson) plexus** into the epidural veins, increasing bleeding during spine operations, which is why spinal surgery frames are designed to let the abdomen hang free. The same plexus explains how tumors can spread to the spine.

**Renal cell carcinoma** characteristically grows as a tumor thrombus into the renal vein and up the IVC, sometimes into the right atrium; resection may require cardiac bypass.

**Budd–Chiari syndrome** (hepatic vein or upper IVC obstruction) causes painful liver enlargement and ascites.

Imaging: Doppler ultrasound, CT venography and MR venography. Point-of-care IVC ultrasound guides fluid therapy in shock.

Treatment in general terms: anticoagulation for thrombosis, catheter-directed clot removal in selected cases, filters when anticoagulation is contraindicated, and surgery for tumor thrombus.

keyPoints: Largest vein; drains legs, pelvis and abdomen into the right atrium
Forms at L5 from the common iliac veins; right of the aorta
Passes the diaphragm's central tendon at T8
Gut blood reaches it only after passing through the liver
Left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta to join it
IVC filters catch leg clots when anticoagulation is unsafe

test.q: At what vertebral level does the IVC pass through the diaphragm?
test.explain: The caval opening at T8 lies in the central tendon; the esophagus passes at T10 and the aorta at T12.

test.q: Relative to the abdominal aorta, the IVC lies:
test.explain: The IVC runs on the right side of the vertebral column, the aorta slightly left.

test.q: Which kidney's vein crosses in front of the aorta?
test.explain: The long left renal vein passes between the aorta and the SMA to reach the IVC.

test.q: A device placed in the IVC to trap clots from the legs is an IVC ______.
test.explain: Used when anticoagulation is unsafe, such as soon after brain surgery.

test.q: Blood from the intestines reaches the IVC by passing first through the:
test.explain: The hepatic portal vein takes gut blood to the liver; hepatic veins then drain into the IVC.
